rationale: Both responses deliver a solid layered architecture, library lists, five well-scoped sprint tickets with tasks and definitions of done, and similar security practices. Both also contain a garbled sanitization-library line. The deciding difference is the hardest requirement: admins creating and removing database fields. A runs live ALTER and DROP TABLE through a whitelisted DSL. That is governed, but it is risky for availability, migrations and ORM model consistency, and its layer redundantly combines Sequelize with Knex. B uses a field-metadata table plus a JSONB column validated at the API layer, which lets admins evolve the schema without runtime DDL or downtime. It soft-deactivates fields so data is preserved. That is the better-practice design. B adds further sound details: opaque, hashed refresh tokens with family revocation on reuse, argon2, mass-assignment protection, cursor pagination, pgBouncer, graceful shutdown and a set-based bulk update. B has a minor inconsistency between all-or-nothing bulk rollback and per-row results, and it narrows users to updating their own records. A's queued bulk jobs, load testing and backup tasks are good, but B's design is stronger overall.
